title: Porodica Mrvice
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar — ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Mrvica adopts Ana; Amira’s café regulars start to feel like family.

vocabulary: Family words: majka, otac, sestra, brat, baba, djed, sin, kći
Café circle: porodica, prijatelj, prijateljica, mačka
grammar: Gender intro: masculine vs feminine nouns
Saying who someone is: Ona je… / On je…
culture: Café regulars as chosen family in Sarajevo
Mrvica as the café’s unofficial boss

grammar.title: Gender intro — he or she words
grammar.explanation: Many Bosnian nouns feel masculine or feminine. A quick beginner tip: words ending in -a are often feminine (majka, sestra, mačka, porodica). Short words without -a are often masculine (otac, brat, sin, djed). You will meet exceptions later — for today, notice the pattern and match moj/moja to it.

grammar.title: Moj / moja and tvoj / tvoja
grammar.explanation: Moj = my before a masculine noun. Moja = my before a feminine noun. Same split for your (informal): tvoj / tvoja. Say Moj brat and Moja sestra. Do not mix them yet — matching gender is the whole game.

grammar.title: Who is who — On je / Ona je
grammar.explanation: Reuse biti from Lesson 2. On je moj prijatelj. Ona je moja prijateljica. Ona je Mrvica — mačka! Point and name people (and one bossy cat) with short lines.

culture.title: Café family — and one small boss
culture.body: In Sarajevo, a good café can feel like a living room. Regulars greet the owner by name, share news, and claim “their” chair. Amira’s place works the same way: Ana, Emir, and the usual guests start to feel like porodica — family you choose. Mrvica the cat patrols the tables, steals warmth, and somehow adopts Ana. Learn the family words, then use them for blood relatives and for the people (and cats) who make a city feel like home.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A — Family words + gender
lessonBlocks.body: Build the tree: majka, otac, sestra, brat, baba, djed, sin, kći. Say each aloud twice. Mark the -a words as feminine in your notes. Add porodica (family) and mačka (cat). Ana draws a tiny family tree in her notebook — then draws Mrvica at the top. Emir laughs: To je porodica Mrvice!
tips: -a endings often = feminine for this lesson’s nouns
kći needs ć — use the accent button

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B — Moj / moja at Amira’s
lessonBlocks.body: Claim people with possessives: Moj prijatelj Emir. Moja prijateljica Amira. Moja mačka? — Mrvica decides that Ana is hers. Practice pairs: Moj otac / Moja majka, Tvoj brat / Tvoja sestra. Walk the café and point: Ona je Amira. On je Emir. Ona je Mrvica. Today’s win is short true sentences, not a full case chart.
tips: Kit: Moj… · Moja… · On je… · Ona je…
Match moj/moja to the noun’s gender

conversation.title: Porodica za stolom

lines.speaker: Ana

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Moja sestra je u Americi. Brat? Ne.
lines.english: My sister is in America. Brother? No.

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.english: Good. We are a little family!

lines.speaker: Ana

funFacts.title: Baba and djed
funFacts.body: Baba is grandmother and djed is grandfather in everyday Bosnian. You will also hear variants in families — learn these two first; they open a lot of stories.

funFacts.title: Prijatelj vs prijateljica
funFacts.body: Friend splits by gender: prijatelj (male), prijateljica (female). Ana calls Emir prijatelj and Amira prijateljica — useful from day one of real friendships.

funFacts.title: Mrvica means little crumb
funFacts.body: A perfect name for a café cat who believes every lap and every lokum crumb is hers.

funFacts.title: Chosen family at the table
funFacts.body: Calling café regulars porodica is half joke, half truth. Warmth is part of the language lesson.

questions.explanation: Sestra is feminine, so moja sestra.

questions.question: Mrvica is a…
questions.explanation: Mrvica je mačka — the café cat.

questions.question: ‘Porodica’ means…
questions.explanation: Porodica = family — blood family or café family.
